title: Treasury Trading at the Close - Liberty Street Economics
gist: New York Fed researchers show that U.S. Treasury trading is increasingly concentrated around fixed-income index 'strike' pricing times, and that when Bloomberg Barclays moved its strike time from 3 p.m. to 4 p.m. ET in January 2021, Treasury market activity abruptly and durably relocated to the new time, especially on month-end index-rebalancing days.

insights.claim: Overall U.S. Treasury security trading volume is about 58 percent higher on the last trading day of the month than on other days.
insights.speaker: Henry Dyer
insights.so_what: Month-end is a structurally predictable high-volume, high-liquidity window in Treasuries that large traders and index-tracking funds can plan around for execution.
insights.quote: overall Treasury security trading volume is about 58 percent higher on the last trading day of the month than on other days
insights.locator: End-of-Month Trading, Index Rebalancing, and Index Strike Times

insights.claim: The authors conjecture that the sharply increased concentration of Treasury trading on month-end days over the past decade reflects the growth of assets managed relative to fixed-income indexes, most of which are rebalanced at month-end.
insights.speaker: Henry Dyer
insights.so_what: As passive and index-benchmarked fixed-income AUM keeps growing, month-end Treasury volume concentration and the associated liquidity dynamics should keep intensifying.
insights.locator: End-of-Month Trading, Index Rebalancing, and Index Strike Times

insights.claim: On the last trading day of the month in 2025, the half-hour window from 3:45 to 4:15 p.m. ET accounts for more than one quarter of that day's total Treasury trading activity on average, with roughly half of that volume packed into just the five minutes from 3:55 to 4:00 p.m.
insights.speaker: Henry Dyer
insights.so_what: A single five-minute window (3:55-4:00 p.m. on month-end days) now absorbs an outsized share of daily Treasury liquidity, raising execution-timing risk and opportunity for traders who must transact near the close on those days.
insights.quote: The half-hour interval between 3:45 and 4:15 p.m. thus accounts for more than one quarter of total daily activity on month-end days in 2025, on average, with about half of that between 3:55 and 4:00 p.m. alone.
insights.locator: Effects Are Changing the Intraday Pattern of Activity

insights.claim: On month-end days, the share of Treasury trading volume clustered in the ten minutes around the 4 p.m. strike rose from an average of 11.6 percent in 2021 to 20.4 percent in 2025, meaning roughly one-fifth of a month-end day's entire volume now trades in that single ten-minute window.
insights.speaker: Henry Dyer
insights.so_what: This concentration level implies material price-impact and slippage risk clustered at a known, recurring instant each month, which could be a source of anomalous volatility or an exploitable liquidity pocket.
insights.locator: Effects More Pronounced on the Last Day of the Month

insights.claim: On January 14, 2021, Bloomberg Barclays (now called Bloomberg Fixed Income Indices), one of the largest providers of fixed-income indexes, changed the official pricing 'strike' time for its U.S. dollar-denominated indexes from 3 p.m. to 4 p.m. ET.
insights.speaker: Henry Dyer
insights.so_what: A benchmark administrator's unilateral pricing-convention decision, not an exchange rule, is what actually times a large share of Treasury market activity — a market-structure lever outside issuer or regulator control worth tracking for other asset-class index providers.
insights.locator: End-of-Month Trading, Index Rebalancing, and Index Strike Times

insights.claim: Reports suggest Bloomberg's rationale for moving its index strike time to 4 p.m. was to reduce tracking error for funds that are required to price their portfolios using 4 p.m. prices, such as mutual funds calculating net asset value.
insights.speaker: Henry Dyer
insights.so_what: Fund tracking-error incentives can trigger changes to benchmark mechanics that then reshape market-wide trading patterns, a second-order channel investors don't typically monitor.
insights.quote: Some reports suggest that one reason for the change was to reduce tracking error for funds that are required to price portfolios using 4 p.m. prices.
insights.locator: End-of-Month Trading, Index Rebalancing, and Index Strike Times

insights.claim: The authors conclude that index pricing conventions materially shape when U.S. Treasury trading occurs during the day.
insights.speaker: Henry Dyer
insights.so_what: Traders, risk managers, and market-structure regulators should treat benchmark strike-time conventions as a primary driver of intraday Treasury liquidity timing, not a footnote.
insights.quote: These results provide strong evidence that index pricing conventions materially shape when Treasury trading occurs.

insights.claim: Before 2021, 3 p.m. was the Treasury market's de facto closing convention partly because open-outcry trading in Treasury futures ended at 3 p.m. and because it gave a lead time before mutual funds' 4 p.m. net asset value production.
insights.speaker: Henry Dyer
insights.so_what: Legacy market-close conventions rooted in now-defunct trading mechanics (open-outcry futures) can persist for years before being displaced by a benchmark provider's operational decision.
insights.locator: End-of-Month Trading, Index Rebalancing, and Index Strike Times

insights.claim: Across all trading days, the share of daily Treasury volume in the ten minutes around 3 p.m. rose from an average of 2.3 percent in 2016 to 3.4 percent in 2020; after Bloomberg's strike-time change, the share around 4 p.m. instead rose from an average of 2.5 percent in 2021 to 3.5 percent in 2025.
insights.speaker: Henry Dyer
insights.so_what: The magnitude of the pre/post shift confirms the strike-time change caused a durable, multi-year reallocation of trading activity rather than a temporary blip.
insights.locator: Trading Increasingly Concentrates at the Close

insights.claim: In 2016, intraday Treasury trading volume spiked at the 8:30 a.m. and 10 a.m. release times of macroeconomic announcements, around 1 p.m. when auction results were released, and around the 3 p.m. strike; by 2025 the 4 p.m. spike is far more pronounced and volume shares are higher across essentially the entire 3:10 p.m. to 5:05 p.m. window.
insights.speaker: Henry Dyer
insights.so_what: Anyone modeling Treasury intraday liquidity or volatility patterns from older (pre-2021) data would be using a stale timing map; the late-afternoon window has become structurally more important.
insights.locator: Effects Are Changing the Intraday Pattern of Activity

insights.claim: Because the U.S. Treasury market is over-the-counter with no exchange-mandated closing time, index providers have sole discretion over what time of day to set closing prices, unlike in the equity market where an exchange fixes the close.
insights.speaker: Henry Dyer
insights.so_what: This discretionary close is a structural difference from equities that makes Treasury market timing dynamics vulnerable to being reset by a single administrator's decision, as happened in 2021.
insights.locator: End-of-Month Trading, Index Rebalancing, and Index Strike Times

insights.claim: The growing, predictable concentration of Treasury trading in narrow windows around index strike times, especially at month-end, creates a recurring, forecastable liquidity event that market participants needing to transact near the close can anticipate and plan execution around.
insights.speaker: Henry Dyer
insights.so_what: Execution desks and liquidity providers can position ahead of the month-end 3:55-4:00 p.m. window, where price impact and volume are both unusually elevated.

insights.claim: Because a single major index provider's strike-time change in 2021 durably 're-timed' a large share of Treasury market activity, a similar decision by another major fixed-income index provider in the future could again abruptly reshape when Treasury liquidity concentrates during the day.
insights.speaker: Henry Dyer
insights.so_what: Market-structure watchers should monitor announcements of index strike-time changes from major benchmark providers as a potential catalyst for shifts in intraday Treasury liquidity and volatility timing.
